cues.text: Let's turn now to Kanban and flow.
Kanban is a method built around a handful of connected ideas.
It visualises workflow, so that everyone can see the work and where it sits.
It limits work in progress, which is usually shortened to WIP.
It manages flow, meaning it pays attention to how smoothly work moves from start to finish.
It makes policies explicit, so the rules the team works by are written down rather than assumed.
It uses feedback loops, and it improves collaboratively.
Now picture the board, because the board is where these ideas become visible.
Work moves through five columns, from left to right.
First is Backlog.
Then Ready.
Then In progress, which carries a WIP limit of three.
Then Review, which carries a WIP limit of two.
And finally Done.
So at any moment, no more than three items can be in progress, and no more than two can be in review.
That limit is the heart of the method.
The rule that makes the limits work is this: pull new work only when capacity exists.
Nobody pushes work onto the team.
When there is room in a column, a team member pulls the next item in.
If a column is full, nothing new enters it.
What happens when something gets stuck?
Blocked items are made visible on the board.
And the team's response is to swarm to resolve the bottleneck, rather than start endless new work.
In other words, when something is stuck, the team gathers around it and clears it, instead of piling up more half-finished items.
To watch flow over time, Kanban teams use a cumulative flow diagram.
This diagram shows how many items sit in each state across time.
The signal to look for is a widening band.
If the band for a particular state grows wider, that means items are accumulating there, and that points toward a bottleneck.
One more point about this method.
Kanban does not require fixed sprints, and it does not require prescribed Scrum roles.
Instead, cadence and service policies can be defined by the team.
Now let us compare Kanban with Scrum, using a table with three columns: Dimension, Scrum, and Kanban.
There are five rows.
The first row is Cadence.
Scrum uses timeboxed sprints.
Kanban uses continuous flow.
The second row is Planning.
In Scrum, planning centres on the Sprint Goal and the backlog.
In Kanban, planning happens through replenishment, guided by capacity and priorities.
The third row is Work control.
In Scrum, control comes from sprint focus.
In Kanban, it comes from explicit WIP limits.
The fourth row is Roles.
Scrum has specific accountabilities.
Kanban has no prescribed role change, meaning it does not ask the team to adopt new roles.
The fifth row is Fit.
Scrum fits product increments and a shared goal.
Kanban fits support and operations work, where arrivals vary.
Finally, do not treat these as rival camps with nothing in common.
Both can use visual boards, continuous improvement and incremental releases.
There is also Scrumban, which combines selected practices from the two.
So how do you choose?
Base the choice on workload variability, interruptions, dependencies and team needs.
And two cautions to finish.
Do not assume that Scrum forbids all changes.
And do not assume that Kanban lacks deadlines.
